sentences.text: Researchers examined 102 adolescents aged 10 to 17, dividing them into two groups based on recent exposure to fine air particles relative to a 9 micrograms per cubic meter limit, while measuring fear through sweat levels, avoidance behaviors, and self-reported feelings.
Participants with higher exposure exhibited a stronger return of fear when the threat was absent, indicated by elevated sweat levels and persistent feelings of fear.

Brain imaging performed on a smaller group of 68 participants revealed that the high-exposure group had more activity in the right amygdala during learning and safety phases, and in the left insula during the recall phase.
The authors suggest that higher air pollution exposure is linked to changes in how fear is processed, which may be a way air pollution contributes to anxiety.
